thread.title: Apple: What The Past And Present Tell Us About The Future - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Logan Kane
title: Apple: What The Past And Present Tell Us About The Future - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) has massively rewarded those who took the risk of owning the stock over time. We also know that Apple shareholders have had some nervous years along the ride. Despite the volatility seen in the stock, the company's fundamentals are solid. The volatility has a lot to do with who your fellow shareholders are and not as much to do with Apple's profits and revenue. While Apple hasn't done what I initially expected it to do this fall, the stock is an even better long-term buy now than it was a couple of months ago.
Apple has seen a decent amount of volatility over time To illustrate this point, I built a graph of the last 10 years of Apple which shows the cumulative drawdowns in the stock. During this time, had you bought and hold AAPL, you'd be up over six times your original investment plus dividends, even after the 20+ percent drop since the most recent high.
AAPL data by YCharts
During this period, you would have had to endure drawdowns of 60 percent during the 2008 crisis, 40 percent in 2013, close to 30 percent in 2016, and over 25 percent now.
Yet even with all the volatility, the last 10 years were less volatile than 1998 to 2008.
AAPL data by YCharts
Contrast this with the graph of price appreciation in Apple since 1998.
AAPL data by YCharts
This is quite a different picture! Despite the frequent drawdowns, Apple's stock has grown so much that if you had any allocation to it at all, it would have taken over your portfolio. The big drawdowns of years past look tiny compared to the appreciation of the stock. They ultimately are, but when you're in the middle of one of them, it can be a little hard to keep in perspective.
Despite the crazy drawdowns, had you held, you'd be up over 380 times your original investment in 20 years.
Wall Street analysts are quick with the drumbeat, saying Apple is done innovating, Tim Cook is trying to hide the iPhone decline from them, Buffett is wrong, China will ruin Apple, Trump will ruin Apple, etc.
I think there's a tendency, in general, to look for a narrative to try to explain the supply and demand dynamic for the stock market when sometimes there isn't a clear-cut reason for it besides sentiment. While I'm sure you can dig up old articles "justifying" each drawdown in Apple's stock, there's never been a time since the iPod launched when you could go to the Apple store and have it not be busy. Growth expectations have changed, but Apple has made tons of money since taking Steve Jobs back in 1997.
I went to the Apple store the other day here in Fort Worth. As always, the store was packed. Bears will discount this type of analysis, but I've found an intuitive and strong correlation between sociological phenomena like fashion trends and product popularity with stock prices in the consumer discretionary sector.
The psychology of Apple shareholders I argued in an earlier article that some of the price behavior in Apple's stock can be explained by the disposition effect .
The premise of the disposition effect is simple. Apple stock has gone up so much and is owned by so many retail investors that their behavior distorts the price of the stock. For example, if you had a 5 percent weighting of Apple in 1998 and invested the rest in SPY , AAPL would have grown to close to 90 percent of your portfolio. If you owned a portfolio of individual stocks, Apple would be closer to 100 percent, as you'd inevitably have losers ( two-thirds of individual stocks underperform the market ).
Apple's success puts its shareholders in an unlikely pickle:
1. Do you cash in and buy everything you've ever wanted (i.e., sell into a still reasonable valuation)
2. Do you diversify into other investments? (Winners keep winning and losers keep losing, so you have to be careful not to hurt your returns)
3. Or, do you let it ride?
The answer to the first question is up to you. There probably isn't an Apple shareholder support group out there, but if there were, that's probably what they'd talk about.
The answer to the second question is that tolerating more concentration when a stock in your portfolio keeps going up increases your returns via the momentum effect and plowing money back into losing stocks tends to reduce your returns via the disposition effect. Most investors don't let winners run far enough and instead pile into losers with the gains from their winners. The S&P 500, on the other hand, is market-capitalization weighted and lets the winners ride. This is one of the main reasons I believe investors struggle to beat the S&P 500 index.
The answer to the third question is a qualified yes. Allowing a stock to be something crazy like 90 percent of your portfolio makes it hard to make good decisions when those nasty drawdowns from above happen. Not allowing winners to grow at all rigs your portfolio to underperform the S&P, which allows winners to grow through market-capitalization weighting. A nice balance, in my opinion, is to start positions at a 10-15 percent maximum and let them float up to 35-40 percent of your portfolio before forcing diversification. This backtests nicely for Apple, but also for bubbles that didn't last, like the bitcoin surge and the 1990s' tech bubble.
^NYB data by YCharts
Letting an investment grow to 35-40 percent of your portfolio and diversifying the gains after that would have continually created amazing amounts of wealth from the crypto boom. The trick is to not re-up the allocation if the hot asset starts to fall back down. This introduces an element of trend following to your portfolio, just like the S&P 500 index does.
I believe that a lot of retail investors have chosen to let it ride in Apple, and a lot of those who have tend to sell during drawdowns as they have tons of concentration risk (a kissing cousin to being overleveraged). It's the nature of owning the same stock as a bunch of panicky retail investors to see volatility.
You're going to see more volatility with retail shareholders than if all the other shareholders were, for example, company employees and large institutions. It doesn't mean Apple is going to fail however, and in fact now is a better time to buy than August was.
If you're reading this, feel free to share your story of how much Apple allocation you have in your portfolio and how you got there in the comments. Hearing your stories is my favorite part of this job!
Apple's valuation is fairly low First, earnings estimates:
AAPL data by YCharts
As you can see, earnings estimates have fallen for Apple in past weeks, but not by nearly as much as they rose in August. However, the stock (along with the rest of the Nasdaq) has been priced as if the sky is falling. Apple now trades for roughly 13.4 times current year earnings. It's not a rock-bottom valuation, but it's a significant discount to the S&P 500 at large and qualifies Apple as a value stock in my opinion.
Much ink has been spilled over Apple's push to monetize the iPhone via service revenue. I actually like the strategy, and while I think transparency on iPhone unit sales is better than opacity, I respect Cook's decision to stop sharing unit sales numbers. Apple's logic is that its job is to maximize revenue, not unit sales.
It's a real problem to try to run a public company for the long term and be judged based on quarterly results.
Also, don't forget that Apple continually buys back stock. The drop in share price allows it to retire more shares, thereby giving a boost to EPS. This helps put a soft floor under Apple's share price.
Services growth is for real - and is in the early innings Apple's crown jewel is its users. It's apparently getting $12 billion in cash in 2019 alone from Google (NASDAQ: GOOG ) (NASDAQ: GOOGL ) for the rights to the default search engine on Safari. That's $2.55 per share for those of you keeping score!
If Apple focuses on innovating more and not worrying about hitting sell-side iPhone unit sales targets, then it could catch Wall Street by surprise. Not every product that Apple launches succeeds, but it has barely scratched the surface of the money it can make off its ecosystem. There are yet to be exploited opportunities in advertising, app sales, storage, health, and more. Consider this fact for a second: Apple is cheaper than Amazon ( AMZN ) based on its service revenue alone, with similar growth potential from the services business. At that point, you get the hardware (iPhone/Mac/Watch) business for free.
Bears argue that iPhone revenue is done growing for good and that Apple's net income has peaked. I don't agree. With the stock at roughly 13 times earnings, the upside is asymmetric and the downside is limited, especially after counting dividends, buybacks, and Apple's still massive pile of net cash.
Conclusion If you own a lot of Apple in your portfolio, I hope this will help you sleep better. If you don't own any Apple, consider buying it or getting exposure through VGT or QQQ . Analyst expectations are low, and the American consumer is strong going into the holiday season. If Christmas sales come in better than expected and the services thesis continues to play out, look for a surprising pop in the price of Apple shares.
Apple likely won't make it to my $240 price target by January, but the stock deserves to be a lot closer to $240 than $180.
